opus-5.5.text:
I think pricing should ultimately reflect value delivered rather than just tokens consumed. But to get there, we first have to be honest about where the industry is today.

Right now, most of us price by tokens. It's simple and transparent, and it maps roughly onto our compute costs. That made sense when models mainly answered single questions. But as models move toward reasoning and agentic work, where one task might involve long chains of thought, many tool calls, and a lot of back-and-forth, token pricing starts to feel misaligned. A user doesn't care how many tokens the model "thought" with. They care whether the bug got fixed or the report got written. And sometimes the model that burns more tokens is actually the cheaper one, because it gets the job done on the first try.

So I see a few forces at play. The first is cost. Training and inference efficiency keep improving, through better architectures, sparsity, and engineering at every layer of the stack. When we can genuinely bring costs down, I think we should pass that on to users. Lower prices expand what people can build, and that grows the whole pie. I've never thought of low pricing as purely a marketing move. If your efficiency is real, it's a strategy you can sustain.

The second force is differentiation. Not every task needs the strongest model. There should be tiers: a fast, cheap model for high-volume simple work, and a premium price for frontier capability on hard problems. Charging the same for everything is wasteful for both sides.

The third is the longer-term direction. I think we'll gradually see more outcome-based or task-based pricing, especially for agents. You pay per completed task, or per unit of work, the way you'd pay a contractor. That's harder to do. You have to define what "done" means and absorb the variance in compute yourself. But it aligns incentives much better. It pushes model builders to be efficient instead of verbose.

What I'd caution against is a pure race to the bottom that isn't backed by real cost advantages. If prices fall below what's sustainable, labs end up cutting corners on research, and that hurts everyone in the long run. Healthy pricing should let you keep investing in the next generation of models while making today's models as accessible as possible.

r001.rationale: It says pricing should reflect the value delivered and describes charging for completed tasks or work.

r002.rationale: It mentions agentic work and tool calls but does not identify post-training as a way to improve understanding of agent frameworks.

fable-5.1.text:
Pricing is actually one of the things I've thought about the most, because it's not really a business question, it's a technology question in disguise.

The cost of a model is basically the cost of inference. So if you can bring inference cost down by an order of magnitude through architecture, through MoE, through things like multi-head latent attention, through better serving infrastructure, then your pricing floor drops with it. When we priced things at a fraction of what the market was charging, people assumed we were subsidizing. We weren't, or at least not in the way they imagined. The price reflected what the model actually cost us to run, plus a reasonable margin. The surprising thing to people was that the cost could be that low.

So my first principle is: price should track real marginal cost, not the perceived value of "intelligence." If you price far above cost because you think AI is magical, you're leaving a gap that someone more efficient will walk through. And you're also slowing adoption. A lot of applications only become viable when calling a model is cheap enough that developers stop thinking about each call.

The second principle is simplicity. Developers hate pricing they can't predict. Per-token pricing, input and output separately, maybe a discount for cache hits because that genuinely reflects lower cost, that's enough. Every additional tier or hidden fee just creates friction.

And the third thing, which I think gets overlooked: low prices force discipline on you as a research team. If you know you have to serve this model at a very low price, you can't afford sloppy architecture. It pushes you to find the efficiency gains. In that sense, pricing is a signal of how good your engineering is, not just a go-to-market decision.

The uncomfortable part is that the market keeps moving. What's cheap this year is expensive next year. So I don't think of any price as permanent. I think of it as the current readout of where the technology is, and the goal is to keep pushing that number down while the capability goes up.

r001.rationale: The response says pricing should track real marginal cost rather than the perceived value of intelligence; it does not propose pricing based on the value the model ultimately produces.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention post-training or improved understanding of agent frameworks.

astra-6.text:
I think pricing should reflect both the cost of running a model and the value it creates for users. A simple task shouldn’t cost the same as a difficult problem that requires much more computation. So it makes sense to offer different models and different levels of reasoning at different prices.

But pricing also needs to be predictable. Users should be able to understand what they’re paying for and control their spending. For developers, charging by tokens is a practical starting point, though token counts don’t necessarily tell you how useful an answer is.

Ultimately, I’d like basic AI capabilities to be very affordable, so more people can experiment and build with them. More demanding capabilities can carry a premium, but that premium should correspond to a meaningful improvement in results.

r001.rationale: It says pricing should reflect the value the model creates for users.

r002.rationale: It does not identify post-training or improved understanding of agent frameworks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think pricing should reflect the value a model delivers, while keeping the cost of trying it low. Charging by tokens is straightforward, but users ultimately care about whether the model solves their problem. A cheaper model that needs several attempts may cost more in practice than a stronger model that gets it right once.

For developers, I’d want transparent usage pricing and predictable costs. For more complex tasks, pricing could move toward completed tasks or outcomes, provided those outcomes can be clearly defined and verified. And I think capable models should remain affordable enough for individuals and small teams to experiment with them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says pricing should reflect the value a model delivers and whether it solves the user's problem.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss post-training or improved understanding of agent frameworks.
